opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's great to be here.

I think AI changes business at a much deeper level than previous technology waves. With the PC, the internet, and mobile, we mostly digitized information and connected people. We made existing processes faster and cheaper. AI is different because it changes who, or what, does the thinking and the work.

I'd describe it in three layers.

The first is the cost structure. For most of history, intelligence was the scarcest and most expensive resource in any company. You hired experts, analysts, engineers, designers, and their time was the bottleneck. Now the marginal cost of a certain kind of intelligence, like writing code, summarizing documents, answering customers, or drafting a design, is approaching zero. When something scarce becomes abundant, the whole economics of an industry gets reorganized. It's a bit like what electricity did to physical labor.

The second is the shape of the organization. Companies have been built around layers of people coordinating information: middle management, reporting, approvals. Agents can now take over much of that coordination. So I think we'll see much smaller teams creating very large value, maybe companies with ten people doing what used to take a thousand. The boundary of the firm, which economists like Coase explained through transaction costs, will move, because AI dramatically lowers those transaction costs.

The third, and to me the most important, is that the product itself changes. In the past, software was a tool. You click, it responds. Now, AI is becoming a collaborator, and soon an autonomous actor. Business models move from selling tools or seats toward selling outcomes. You don't pay for a piece of software; you pay for the task getting done. That is a fundamental shift in how value is defined and captured.

And it doesn't stop at the digital world. At Tsinghua AIR, we spend a lot of time on what I call physical AI and biological AI: autonomous driving, robotics, and AI for drug discovery and life sciences. When intelligence enters atoms and molecules, not just bits, it touches manufacturing, transportation, healthcare, which are the biggest parts of the economy.

That said, I'd add a caution. Technology moves fast, but businesses and society adapt more slowly. Data, trust, safety, regulation, and how people's jobs transition all matter enormously. The companies that win won't simply be the ones with the biggest model; they'll be the ones that redesign their entire workflow and value proposition around AI, while managing risk responsibly. So, in short, AI isn't just a new tool for business. It's a new kind of production factor, and it forces us to rethink what a company is.

r001.rationale: The response says AI changes business at a deeper, fundamental level and forces companies to rethink how they operate, contradicting the claim that its essence has not changed.

r002.rationale: It describes intelligence becoming far cheaper and says teams of ten may create value that once required a thousand people, clearly communicating a substantial productivity increase.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the essence of business doesn't actually change. Business is still about creating value for customers and capturing some of that value in a sustainable way. What AI changes is the cost structure and the speed at which that value gets created.

Think about what happened with the internet. It didn't change what commerce is, but it collapsed the cost of distribution and information to nearly zero. AI is doing something similar, but to intelligence itself. The marginal cost of analysis, of writing, of design, of coding, of customer service, is dropping very fast. When a key input becomes almost free, everything built on top of it has to be rethought.

So I see three layers of change. The first is efficiency. Companies use AI to do what they already do, but faster and cheaper. That's where most enterprises are today, and honestly it's necessary but not very interesting. The second layer is new products and new experiences. Things that were impossible before become possible, like a personal tutor for every child or a driver in every car. The third layer, and the most profound one, is organizational. If a small team with good models can do what used to require a thousand people, then the shape of the firm changes. The boundary of the company, the role of middle management, the way we think about headcount as a measure of scale, all of that gets questioned.

At Baidu I saw this starting to happen with autonomous driving. The product was not a car, it was a system that learns. The company becomes a loop between data, models, and users. And I'd say the companies that will win are not the ones with the best models, because models will become commodities. They're the ones that figure out how to put the model inside a real feedback loop with real customers, and compound that over time.

So the essence stays the same. The physics of the game change.

r001.rationale: The response says the essence of business “doesn't actually change” and later that “the essence stays the same.”

r002.rationale: It says AI lets companies do existing work “faster and cheaper” and sharply lowers the marginal cost of analysis, writing, design, coding, and customer service, communicating a substantial productivity increase.

astra-6.text:
I think AI changes business at three levels. First, it improves efficiency. You can automate routine tasks, help people make decisions, and reduce the cost of delivering a product or service. That is where many companies begin, because the benefits are relatively easy to measure.

Second, it changes the product itself. Software becomes more interactive and more personalized. Instead of asking the customer to learn how to use a system, the system increasingly learns what the customer needs. That opens up new services and new business models.

Third, it changes how a company organizes its work. When intelligence becomes widely available, you have to rethink which decisions people make, what you delegate to machines, and how you establish accountability. Simply adding AI to an existing process may give you an incremental improvement. Redesigning the process can create a much bigger change.

But the fundamental purpose of business is still to create value for customers. Intelligence becomes cheaper; understanding which problems are worth solving, earning trust, and executing well remain essential. So the key question for a business leader is: with these new capabilities, what can we do for our customers that we could not do before?

r001.rationale: It says the fundamental purpose of business remains creating value for customers, despite AI changing products and work processes.

r002.rationale: It describes efficiency gains and lower delivery costs, but does not clearly state that AI substantially increases productivity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI changes business at three levels. First, it improves efficiency. You can automate routine work, help people make better decisions, and reduce the cost of delivering a product or service. That is where many companies begin, because the return is relatively easy to measure.

Second, it changes the product itself. Software becomes more conversational, more personalized, and increasingly capable of taking action. So companies have to rethink what they sell and what customers actually need from them.

The third level is the business model and the organization. If intelligence becomes widely available, what makes your company unique? It may be your understanding of an industry, your customer relationships, or your ability to integrate technology into a real workflow. Simply having access to an AI model will not be enough.

But I would distinguish between the essence of business and the way business operates. The essence is still creating value for customers and earning their trust. AI changes how you do that, potentially very dramatically. The key question for a business leader is: what can we now do for our customers that we could not do before?

r001.rationale: The response says the essence of business is still creating customer value and earning trust; AI changes how businesses do that.

r002.rationale: It says AI improves efficiency and can reduce costs, but does not clearly state that AI substantially increases productivity.
